page.title: Creative Operations Process: Stages, Tools, Metrics
page.description: Learn the seven stages of a creative operations process, the tools teams use, and the metrics that prove it works.
page.h1: What is the creative operations process?
page.definition: A creative operations process is a repeatable workflow that moves work from intake through brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting with one owner and one output at every stage.
page.quick_answer: Map your work into seven stages, assign one owner per stage, and track cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate and capacity use each month.

sections.h2: What are the seven stages every creative request must pass through?

blocks.p: The seven stages are intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting, each with a single owner and a tangible output.

ol: Intake: capture request, assign priority, log in work management tool
Brief: complete template, confirm scope, get stakeholder sign-off
Production: create assets, follow brand system, store versions in asset manager
Review: route to reviewers in video or design review tool, collect timestamped feedback
Approval: final sign-off from brand voice and legal, record decision
Publishing: push to CMS or social scheduler, tag for analytics
Reporting: measure cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate, capacity use

sections.h2: Which tools support each stage without creating duplicate work?

blocks.p: Choose one tool per category so handoffs stay clean and data flows forward.

sections.h2: How do you measure whether the process is actually faster?

blocks.p: Track four core metrics every month and compare them against the baseline you set in the first ninety days.

ul: Cycle time: working days from approved brief to publish
Revision rounds: count of review cycles per asset
On-time rate: percentage of deliverables hitting the committed date
Capacity use: planned hours versus actual hours per producer

sections.h2: What does a realistic timeline look like for a long-form article?

blocks.p: A typical long-form article takes five to ten working days from approved brief to publish, with most of that time spent in review.

ul: Day one to two: production draft
Day three to five: stakeholder review and revisions
Day six: final approval and CMS load
Day seven to ten: buffer for legal or compliance checks

sections.h2: When should you add AI to the workflow and what guardrails apply?

blocks.p: Insert AI at research, drafting and image variant steps, but enforce a human-in-the-loop rule so every output has a named approver before it moves forward.

ul: Research and outlines: ChatGPT or Claude
Image variants: Adobe Firefly or Canva
Hand-offs between tools: Zapier or Make
Approval gate: a person signs off before publishing

sections.h2: How do you staff the process when the team is small?

blocks.p: A full creative ops team has five roles, but small teams combine them into one producer who owns the calendar, briefs, review routing and reporting.

faq.q: What is the first step to implement a creative operations process?
faq.a: Start by mapping current requests into the seven stages, then assign one owner per stage and choose a single work management tool to host the workflow.

faq.q: How long before the new process shows measurable improvement?
faq.a: Run the process for ninety days while tracking cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate and capacity use; that window is long enough to see a trend and short enough to adjust.

faq.q: Can the same process handle video, design and written content?
faq.a: Yes, the seven stages stay the same; only the review tool changes, such as Frame.io for video and Figma for design, while the work management layer remains constant.

faq.q: What happens if a stakeholder skips the brief stage?
faq.a: Treat an incomplete brief as a blocked intake; the work management tool should prevent the request from moving to production until every required field is approved.
